title: One God, three persons
hook: Father, Son and Holy Spirit: one God in a communion of love

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bara: the world made, meant, and very good. Your line was very good.

In a Russian monastery, around six hundred years ago, a monk named Andrei Rublev painted an icon of God as Trinity. Three angels sit around a table, under a tree. It's the Genesis story of three visitors at Abraham's tent. They look almost identical, long-winged and gentle-faced, each head tilting toward the others. Nobody sits at the head of the table. Their hands and eyes make a circle. And at the front, facing you, there's an open place, as if someone has been invited in. Christians have looked at it for centuries to glimpse today's word.
screen: `RUBLEV'S ICON, AROUND 1420.` → `THREE AT ONE TABLE.` → `AN OPEN PLACE FACING YOU.`

segments.voice: Trinity comes from the Latin trinitas, a three-in-oneness. A North African writer named Tertullian used it around the year 200. Surprise: the word isn't in the Bible. The three names are, again and again. At Jesus's baptism: the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice from heaven. At the end of Matthew, Jesus sends his friends out, "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Name, singular. Three, and one. Paul ends a letter with a blessing still said in churches: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." Christians say the Trinity is one God in three persons: not three gods, and not one God wearing three masks. The councils spent decades finding words for it, and Christians are the first to call it a mystery. People try pictures, water as ice, liquid and steam, or a three-leaf shamrock, but theologians usually say every picture goes wrong somewhere. So why hold it at all? One answer starts from First John: God is love. Love needs someone to love, the reasoning goes. If God is Trinity, then before anything was made, God was already a communion: giving, receiving, sharing, forever. That's what Rublev painted: a circle of love, with a place left open. Some Christians, such as Unitarians, Jehovah's Witnesses and Latter-day Saints, understand God differently. For the Catholic, Orthodox and historic Protestant churches, the Trinity is at the center of the faith.
screen: `TRINITAS: NOT A BIBLE WORD.` · `THREE NAMES, ONE NAME.` · `A MYSTERY NO PICTURE HOLDS.` · `GOD IS LOVE, SO GOD IS COMMUNION.` · then, large: `THE COMMUNION OF THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Think of three people who love each other, maybe you and two friends, a parent and two children, and picture them at one table. Notice how the love doesn't split into pieces; it goes round, and gets bigger with each person. If you pray, use Paul's blessing: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost. If you don't, rest in the picture of that table.
Trinity. Father, Son and Holy Spirit: one God, three persons, a communion of love.
Your line: god is a communion. Three at one table, and an open place. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Christians make the sign of the cross "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit," and many churches celebrate Trinity Sunday, the Sunday after Pentecost.

notes: Editor review (282-299 pass): cut 'many people call the most beautiful ever made'; Tertullian 'made the word popular' changed to 'used it in Latin, around the year 200'; 'spent a century' made 'spent decades'; the love-needs-someone argument is now framed as one answer rather than stated by the narrator; 'most churches' replaced with the churches named.
Rublev's Trinity: dated c. 1411 or 1425–27; script says 'around six hundred years ago' and 'around 1420'. Confirm.
Tertullian (c. 200) is the earliest surviving Latin use of trinitas; Theophilus of Antioch (c. 180) used trias in Greek. Confirm.

Non-trinitarian groups named (Unitarians, Jehovah's Witnesses, Latter-day Saints) without judgment; whether all describe themselves as Christian varies — Unitarian Universalists may not. Confirm naming.
The 'love needs someone to love' argument is associated with Richard of St Victor and others; given as a common Christian reflection.
The 'three to one table' fork option 'a triangle with an eye' is a later Western symbol; used as a distractor only.
